name: Nagpuria
confidence_why: The only explicit statement, the Nagpuria sketch by Srivastava & Pattanaik (2023) in the Linguistic Survey of India: Jharkhand, says the second syllable of 2-4-syllable words carries the predictable long vowel and is always stressed, and its transcriptions mark the acute on syllable 2 throughout (imá:n, kirá:, kAtá:ri, jAbá:b, po:thí:, ku:Tá:si:, bi:sé:khu:), while the companion Sadan/Sadri sketch by Ghosh & Pattanaik (2023) in the same volume says only that non-phonemic stress goes with long vowels in closed syllables, without examples, and Whitley (1896), Grierson (1903), Datta & Ahirwal (2002) and Uranw & Yadav (2009) say nothing about stress. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Srivastava & Pattanaik 2023 2023.
catalog_citation: Srivastava, S.P. & Ranjita Pattanaik. 2023. Nagpuria. In R. Nakkeerar (ed.), Linguistic Survey of India: Jharkhand, pp. 432-565. Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India. Open scan:https://archive.org/details/PARI.linguistic-survey-of-india--jharkhand

catalog_quote: The length is not phonemic. However, the long vocoids occur in the phonetic level and their occurrences are predictable. The vocoids occurring in the mono- syllabic words are uniformly long; while in disyllabic, tri – syllabic and tetra- syllabic words (available a very few), the vocoids of the second syllable are long. Stress also is a co- occurring feature with the length, i.e., the syllables having long vocoids are always stressed. ... [imá:n] / iman / ‘honesty’ ... [ kirá] / kira / ‘worm’ ... [ kAtá: ri] / kAtari / ‘sugarcane’ ... [gA:dé: la] /gAdela / ‘issueless cow or buffalo’ ... [ku:kú:ro] / kukur/ ‘ dog’ ... [bA:sú:li:] / bAsuli / ‘ small axe ‘ ... [pA:pi΄:ta] /pApita / ‘papaya’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and rides on predictable phonetic vowel length: a monosyllable is long and stressed; in words of two or more syllables the vowel of the second syllable is long and therefore stressed. The section's own transcriptions mark stress on the second syllable of polysyllables ([imá:n] 'honesty', [kirá:] 'worm', [kAtá:ri] 'sugarcane', [geRé:] 'duck', [gA:dé:la] 'issueless cow').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the Nagpuria sketch. The sibling sketch in the same volume (Ghosh & Pattanaik, 'Sadan/Sadri', printed p. 652 = p. 669, same file) gives a different conditioning: 'Length is not phonemic in Sadan/Sadri. Phonetically lengths of vowels are predictable only in the close syllable. Stress: Stress is not phonemic in Sadan/Sadri. It occurs mainly with long vowels in the close syllable.' Both agree stress is non-phonemic and length-linked; they disagree on whether length (hence stress) goes to the second syllable or to closed syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in a phoneme/allophone inventory); nothing on phrase-level prominence. Stress is treated as a phonetic correlate of predictable length, not as an independent prosodic system; the sketch is a government survey description (fieldwork Ranchi and Palamau districts 1978-80, updated 2010), not an instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from the 'Nagpuria' mother-tongue sketch (Srivastava & Pattanaik 2023; fieldwork Ranchi and Palamau districts), i.e. Chotanagpuri Sadri/Nagpuri of the Ranchi plateau, which Glottolog lists under sadr1248 (alternate names Nagpuri, Chota Nagpuri, Sadani). The same 2023 volume carries a separate census-label sketch 'Sadan/Sadri' (Ghosh & Pattanaik, Ranchi district) with a differing conditioning of stress, quoted under exceptions. Uranw & Yadav 2009 describe the Kisaan 'Saadri' of Jhapa, Nepal, a diaspora variety, and are silent on stress. Assam tea-garden Sadri (Saikia 2015, Dey 2011) is not represented in the opened sources.

new_statements.relation_note: Partial disagreement, and about a different regional variety. For disyllables Saikia's verb rule (second syllable) and most transcriptions (ràjá, mèsá, dìmág) match the catalog's '01'. For trisyllables the catalog (from Srivastava) has '010' (second syllable), whereas Saikia's transcriptions are predominantly final '001' (məhìná, tetèŋá, mukʰiyá, čàriyó, bʰarùwá; only janówàr is 010), plus diphthong attraction and a set of initial-accented words that Srivastava's length-based rule does not predict. The thesis describes Sadri as spoken in the tea gardens of Upper Assam ('Bagania Bhasa'), which the author states (ch.1 p.1) 'is different to the one spoken in Chota Nagpur region as it is heavil…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word has one primary accent; monosyllables carry it; in disyllabic verb forms in isolation the primary accent is always on the second syllable; a syllable with a diphthong ('complex peak') takes the primary accent in polysyllables. No general placement rule is stated for other words; the author's own transcriptions (pp.223-226) put the primary accent mostly on the final syllable of di- and trisyllables (ràjá 'king', pàháṛ 'hill', dìmág 'brain', məhìná 'month', tetèŋá 'lizard', mukʰiyá 'chief', čàriyó 'all four', bʰarùwá, əgùwá, bəčàbó 'will save'), on the diphthong syllable wherever it sits (páisà, bə́imàn, pʰə́isəlà, báundarì, brìhəspáit, satànəbbói, məhàdéu), but a residue of plain words is initial-accented (jámùn 'berry', níyə̀m 'rules', ánùsər, íleksòn, ghúŋgì, ádʰuniktà) and janówàr 'animal' is medial, so placement is not fully predictable from the account given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A secondary accent [ ` ] is posited for every word of two or more syllables ('It varies considerably'); words of three or more syllables have exactly one primary and one secondary accent, remaining syllables unaccented. In the transcriptions the secondary usually sits on the initial or pre-tonic syllable (nàráj, bèyakúl, səsùráir) or, when the primary is early, on the final (íleksòn, jámùn, páisà).
new_statements.exceptions: Diphthong syllables attract the main accent; disyllabic-verb rule stated only for isolated verb forms; several initial-accented nouns/loans listed without comment (jámùn, níyə̀m, ánùsər, íleksòn, ádʰuniktà, ghúŋgì).
new_statements.identity_note: Srivastava 1989 describes Nagpuriya (Sadani/Sadri) of Chotanagpur, data collected in Ranchi and Palamau districts (then Bihar, now Jharkhand) and checked in Jashpur, Singhbhum and border areas; the investigator is a Bhojpuri mother-tongue speaker and made no tape recordings. Saikia 2015 describes Sadri as the lingua franca of the tea-tribe (Adivasi) communities in the tea gardens of Upper Assam ('Bagania Bhasa'), informants with Munda/Oraon/Kharia surnames, and explicitly says this variety differs from Chotanagpur Sadri through heavy Assamese and Bengali influence; it falls under sadr1248 but is not the Nagpuria of the catalog record.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Vowel length is allophonic and predictable: the vowel of a monosyllable is long, and in words of two, three or four syllables the vowel of the second syllable is long; stress co-occurs with length, so the second syllable (the only syllable in monosyllables) is always stressed. The allophone statements on pp.65-68 formalize this: long [i: e: a: ə: o: u:] occur in #(C)_(C)# and in (C)V(C)(C)(C)_(C).., short allophones elsewhere (examples pi:ṭh 'back', bani: 'saying', abri:k 'now', mistri: 'mason', papi:ta 'papaya', chuti:hara 'debased pot', dusma:n 'enemy', bədo:hi).
new_statements.exceptions: Tetra-syllabic words said to be very few; sentence-level 'intonation and stress' in interrogatives explicitly left unanalysed (p.321). No lexical exceptions given.

readall_conflicts: No new source could be opened, so no new disagreement was found. The standing tension already on record remains: the Nagpuria sketch (Srivastava & Pattanaik 2023, LSI Jharkhand p. 459) ties stress to predictable vowel length on the second syllable of 2-4-syllable words, while the Sadan/Sadri sketch in the same volume (Ghosh & Pattanaik 2023, p. 652) says stress is non-phonemic and occurs with long vowels in closed syllables, and the allophone lists contain long vowels outside syllable 2 without a stress mark; Whitley 1896 and Uranw & Yadav 2009 are silent. Srivastava 1989 (Nagpuriya of Ranchi and Palamau, Chotanagpur; the source text later reused in LSI Jharkhand 2023) states a clean rule: the second syllable of any di-, tri- or tetra-syllabic word has the long vowel and is always stressed (monosyllables long and stressed), with no secondary stress and no exceptions. Saikia 2015, describing the Assam tea-garden variety of Sadri (Bagania Bhasa), agrees for disyllables (isolated disyllabic verbs 'always' second-syllable; nouns transcribed ràjá, pàháṛ, dìmág) but her transcriptions of trisyllables are predominantly final-accented (məhìná, tetèŋá, mukʰiyá, čàriyó, bʰarùwá) rather than second-syllable, she adds that a diphthong syllable takes the main accent wherever it is (páisà, bə́imàn, báundarì, brìhəspáit), posits a secondary accent in every polysyllable, and lists several initial-accented words (jámùn, níyə̀m, ánùsər, íleksòn, ádʰuniktà) that neither rule predicts.
